messages.subject: Re: UTM as.telemetry() error + location error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Krystan,
It would be easier to just import the long-lat with a non-default datum="NAD83" argument.
UTM.zone = "17 +north +datum=NAD83" shouldn't be necessary any longer (versus just zone=17).
I want to say that "+north" stopped working in some PROJ versions.
The datum argument can be just the datum name, rather than an entire PROJ string or CRS, like  datum="NAD83". Also, with the datum argument, now you don't need to sneak the datum into the UTM zone column any longer - that would add two datums in the PROJ string. I will add an as.character() call to fix this error, in case anyone supplies a CRS object.
The datum itself, like NAD83, is just the ellipsoid model of the input coordinates (usually long-lat) and any other projection information in the datum argument is not used by as.telemetry.
The projection argument is for the output telemetry object and, by default, it is a 2-point equidistant projection with the  WGS84 datum. It can be made to be anything else that you want, but it needs to be relatively centered on the data and in meters. You can also project the data after importing, rather than during.
You appear to have Argos data with error ellipse information, so as long as you name the columns correctly, as.telemetry should import them and you should see them when you plot the tracking data. Then all you have to do is turn the error model on in the model guess object.
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Occurrence distribution PMF values as weights in regression
messages.subject_clean: Occurrence distribution PMF values as weights in regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I wouldn't do this, nor would I do the kind of RSFs where people make a tight buffer around the data to define the available region. This uses two different estimators - one for the available area and one for the selection - and does not propagate the uncertainty from the first estimate to the second, nor are the first set of parameters fit consistently with how the second set are fitted, and there is often sensitivity to choices made in the first fit. I think integrated SSFs and RSFs make much more sense.

If you annotate the location data with mortality, then you could consider selection like:
~ vegetation + burnt:mortality
for individuals that don't select for burnt habitat but are more likely to die there, and
~ vegetation + burnt + burnt:mortality
for individuals that select for burnt habitat and are more likely to die there, but not
~ vegetation + burnt*mortality
because this includes a mortality adjustment to the intercept term (in ctmm this term will be automatically discarded).

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

I would also look at the distribution of tau[position] home-range crossing timescale estimates, as the longer of those will often indicate non-resident behavior.
In that regard, if the tau[position] estimates are within the normal range, most of these look okay for small DOF estimates, but not the last one - there is a clear mismatch between the asymptote of most of the variogram and of the fitted model, likely from the included migratory points.

Chris

messages.subject: Speed overestimates from camera traps
messages.body_plain:
Hey Chris,

I have gotten CTMM to run on a test deployment for individuals with at least 12 points. Everything has been working well and I have been getting accurate speed measurements. However, when I run my code on all of my cameras and thus every individual my speed estimates for deer are 400 kilometers a day. Am I missing something in the code (colored in red to help) to make it overestimate? Could dt.max be the issue? When I run them individually, there are a multiple outliers with really large speeds.

Thank you!

Code:
library(ctmm)
library(dplyr)
#install.packages("raster")
#install.packages("move")
library(move)
#library(move2)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
#most individuals have less than 10 points (?)

##SETUP##
# Load the data
data <- read.csv("merged_results.csv", header = TRUE)

# Identify sequences with any detection_idx > 0 and exclude them
sequences_to_exclude <- data %>%
  filter(detection_idx > 0) %>%
  distinct(sequence_id) %>%
  pull(sequence_id)  # Creates a vector of sequence_ids to exclude

# Filter the dataset for White-tailed Deer, excluding the identified sequences
filtered_data <- data %>%
  mutate(time = as.POSIXct(timestamp, format = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")) %>%
  filter(common_name == "White-tailed Deer",
         !sequence_id %in% sequences_to_exclude,
         !duplicated(paste0(deployment_id, timestamp))) %>%
  arrange(deployment_id, time) %>%
  rename(id = transect_id, x = world_x, y = world_z)

filtered_data_oneCam <- filtered_data %>%
  filter(deployment_id == filtered_data$deployment_id[[100]])
###### 1CAMS ####
move_obj <- move(x = filtered_data_oneCam$x,
                 y = filtered_data_oneCam$y,
                 time = filtered_data_oneCam$time,
                 proj = "+proj=utm +zone=33 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +north",
                 animal = filtered_data_oneCam$sequence_id)
###### TOTAL
move_obj <- move(x = filtered_data$x,
                 y = filtered_data$y,
                 time = filtered_data$time,
                 proj = "+proj=utm +zone=33 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +north",
                 animal = filtered_data$sequence_id)

# Create a telemetry object using 'transect_id' as the individual identifier
# Here, we use direct column access rather than creating a new 'time' column unnecessarily
telemetry_data <- as.telemetry(move_obj)

# Display the head of the telemetry data to verify
summary(telemetry_data)

###TESTING###
i = 4 #from sequences to the whole camera as an individual animal = "how deer are using the place right in front of the camera", estimate error for the whole grid (WI, find 20 times where deer not moving - avg poosition of points is true position then look at pathagoerm theroem fistance from average point)

GUESS <- ctmm.guess(telemetry_data[[i]], CTMM=ctmm(error=1.19), interactive=FALSE)
FIT   <- ctmm.select(telemetry_data[[i]], verbose=TRUE, GUESS)
#summary(FIT [[1]])
out <- ctmm::speed(FIT[[1]], data = telemetry_data[[i]], dt.max = 600, robust = TRUE) #instantaneous speed from MM, km/day
# outs <- ctmm::speeds(FIT[[1]], data = telemetry_data[[i]], dt.max = 600, robust = TRUE) #speeds at any given location or timestep

###RUNNING###
# Create an empty list to store results
speed_results <- list()

# Loop over each individual in telemetry_data
for (i in seq_along(telemetry_data)) {

  # Check if the individual has enough data points (12 or 13)
  if (nrow(telemetry_data[[i]]) < 12) {  # Set to 12 or 13 based on preference
    message(paste("Skipping individual", i, "due to insufficient data points"))
    next
  }

  # Run ctmm.guess and ctmm.select, with error handling
  GUESS <- try(ctmm.guess(telemetry_data[[i]], CTMM = ctmm(error = 1.19), interactive = FALSE), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(GUESS, "try-error")) {
    message(paste("Error in GUESS for individual", i, "- skipping"))
    next
  }

  FIT <- try(ctmm.select(telemetry_data[[i]], verbose = TRUE, GUESS), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(FIT, "try-error")) {
    message(paste("Error in FIT for individual", i, "- skipping"))
    next
  }

  # Estimate speed, with error handling
  out <- try(ctmm::speed(FIT[[1]], data = telemetry_data[[i]], dt.max = 600, robust = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(out, "try-error")) {
    message(paste("Error in speed estimation for individual", i, "- skipping"))
    next
  }

  # Store the result
  speed_results[[i]] <- out
  message(paste("Completed speed estimation for individual", i))
}

### RESULTS  # The speed_results list will contain results for each individual with sufficient data
head(speed_results)
# Loop through each result in speed_results and print the individual speed estimates and confidence intervals
for (i in seq_along(speed_results)) {
  result <- speed_results[[i]]

  if (!is.null(result) && "CI" %in% names(result)) {
    cat("Individual", i, "Speed Estimate:\n")
    print(result$CI)  # Display the estimate and confidence interval for speed (km/day)
    cat("\n")
  } else {
    cat("Individual", i, "has no valid speed result.\n")
  }
}

###ANSWERS###

# Initialize vectors to store speed estimates and confidence intervals
estimates <- c()
low_CI <- c()
high_CI <- c()

# Loop through speed_results to extract the estimates and confidence intervals
for (result in speed_results) {
  if (!is.null(result) && "CI" %in% names(result) &&
      "speed (kilometers/day)" %in% rownames(result$CI) &&
      all(c("est", "low", "high") %in% colnames(result$CI))) {

    # Extract the "speed (kilometers/day)" row for low, est, and high
    estimates <- c(estimates, result$CI["speed (kilometers/day)", "est"])
    low_CI <- c(low_CI, result$CI["speed (kilometers/day)", "low"])
    high_CI <- c(high_CI, result$CI["speed (kilometers/day)", "high"])

  } else {
    message("Skipping an entry in speed_results due to missing CI data")
  }
}

# Now you can proceed to calculate the average and CI for the extracted estimates
if (length(estimates) > 0) {
  mean_speed <- mean(estimates)
  overall_low_CI <- mean(low_CI)
  overall_high_CI <- mean(high_CI)

  # Calculate the standard error and rigorous CI
  std_error <- sd(estimates) / sqrt(length(estimates))
  ci_lower <- mean_speed - 1.96 * std_error
  ci_upper <- mean_speed + 1.96 * std_error

  # Display results
  cat("Average Speed Estimate:", mean_speed, "km/day\n")
  cat("Average Confidence Interval:", overall_low_CI, "-", overall_high_CI, "km/day\n")
  cat("\nRigorous 95% Confidence Interval:", ci_lower, "-", ci_upper, "km/day\n")
} else {
  message("No valid speed estimates found in speed_results.")
}

#Plots
library(dplyr)
install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)

# Plot speed estimates with confidence intervals
ggplot(speed_results, aes(x = factor(deployment_id), y = speed_est)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.2, color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Speed Estimates by Deployment",
    x = "Deployment ID",
    y = "Speed (km/day)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

####END####

messages.subject: Re: error model using Ornitella units
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob.

The reported RMSE_min is the RMSE under ideal satellite reception (usually HDOP=1). However, those tags did not have informative HDOP values, and the selected error model was the homoskedastic one. Therefore your RMSE would be environmentally dependent.

Following the error vignette, you would run uere.fit() on the calibration data and then uere()<- to calibrate. However, with this model tag, I would definitely do error-model selection and test to see if the HDOP values are informative. There is a good chance that you would want to toss them out (opposite to the vignette example).

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I hope you're doing well. I'm trying to estimate, and compare, the mean speed and directional persistence of daily trajectories of a vulture created from GPS daytime locations recorded every 15 minutes.

The trajectories have gaps because I removed clusters of stationary locations. Some trajectories are as short as 12 locations, with a mean of 22 locations per trajectory. Since my trajectories are segments of daily and daytime flight, I have not found evidence of non-stationary behavior.

Following Noonan et al. (2019), I selected a movement model for each daily trajectory and, for those trajectories with OUF, OUf, or IOU models, I estimated the mean speed (via the speed function). I employed LOOCV as the IC method in ctmm.guess. Please find my code attached.

I wanted to confirm whether it's appropriate to use the CTSD approach (for those trajectories with OUF, OUf, or IOU movement models) despite the small sample sizes.
I also wanted to know if there are any other considerations I should account for in my code, e.g., I’m not using fast = FALSE in speed because I found little difference in the results without it although I have not tested it for too many trajectories.

Any insights would be much appreciated!

Thanks for your help and time,

Paula

Hi Chris (and the ctmm group),

I was wondering if anyone could help me with some issues with RSF interpretation for a model looking at categorical variable effects. I can only really find information on interpreting continuous models, so if anyone could offer some resources/papers that have detail on interpreting categorical models, that would be much appreciated.

I am running an RSF to try to look at broad scale landscape use, looking at range distribution and if habitat can predict this. I am using GPS data from a population of Crowned Eagles and a national landcover dataset, which categorises the country into one of nine different landcover classes.

I have ran a preliminary RSF using rsf.fit with the Riemann integrator, the output of which I have attached below though I'm not entirely sure how to interpret it. From what I understand, category 4 (which is forested land) is being used as a reference category with respect to all other levels, with the insignificant results having much more variance. Forested land is the most used land class, so I appreciate it's probably not the best one to use in the final model. I was thinking about if it's possible to model without a reference category, and wondered if I created binary rasters of each habitat class (1 for habitat class presence and 0 for absence) I could assess each class independently? Would this be appropriate for the model/ do you have any further suggestions?

Happy to attach the code too if that will help. Thanks so much in advance.

Best wishes,
Lara
